text: In equal circles, equal straight-lines subtend equal circumferences. Let $ABC$ and $DEF$ be equal circles, and within them let the equal circumferences $BGC$ and $EHF$ be cut off. And let the straight-lines $BC$ and $EF$ be joined. I say that $BC$ is equal to $EF$.
For let the centers of the circles be found [Prop.~3.1], and let them be (at) $K$ and $L$.
And since the circumference $BGC$ is equal to the circumference $EHF$, the angle $BKC$ is also equal to (angle) $ELF$ [Prop.~3.27].

spans.label: assumption
spans.text: the circumference $BGC$ is equal to the circumference $EHF$

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the angle $BKC$ is also equal to (angle) $ELF$

text: And since the circles $ABC$ and $DEF$ are equal, their radii are also equal [Def.~3.1].
assertion: the radii of circles ABC and DEF are equal

text: So the two (straight-lines) $BK$, $KC$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $EL$, $LF$ (respectively).
assertion: BK and KC equal EL and LF respectively

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the two (straight-lines) $BK$, $KC$ are equal to the two (straight-lines) $EL$, $LF$ (respectively)

assertion: BK,KC and EL,LF contain equal angles

text: Thus, the base $BC$ is equal to the base $EF$ [Prop.~1.4].

spans.label: assertion
spans.text: the base $BC$ is equal to the base $EF$

text: Thus, in equal circles, equal straight-lines subtend equal circumferences. (Which is) the very thing it was required to show.
